questions.text: A client files a complaint with the PRBoA alleging that an architect failed to design according to the Philippine Building Code. The architect responds claiming the client approved the design deviation. At what stage can the PRBoA dismiss the complaint as frivolous?

options.text: Before formal investigation if the response is satisfactory and addresses all points raised in the complaint
Only after formal investigation if evidence supports the architect's claim and disproves the allegations
Before formal investigation if the complaint lacks sufficient factual basis to proceed
Only after a formal hearing and board deliberation involving testimony from both parties and expert witnesses

rationale.a: Response satisfactoriness does not determine frivolousness; factual sufficiency is the standard.
rationale.b: Dismissal for frivolousness may occur before investigation; formal investigation is not required.
rationale.d: Formal hearing is not required for frivolousness dismissal; early threshold determination applies.
rationale.correct: The PRBoA may dismiss a complaint before formal investigation if it lacks sufficient factual basis or is clearly frivolous. The client's allegation (design non-compliance) is factually sufficient to proceed.
rationale.takeaway: PRBoA may dismiss frivolous complaints before formal investigation if lacking factual basis.

questions.text: During an investigative hearing, the complainant (a contractor) testifies that the architect told him the building code "doesn't apply to this project." The architect, through counsel, objects that this is hearsay and inadmissible. How should the PRBoA rule?

options.text: Sustain the objection because hearsay is inadmissible in administrative proceedings, which typically follow strict rules of evidence
Overrule the objection because administrative hearings apply relaxed evidentiary standards
Sustain the objection and require the architect to testify directly, ensuring that the testimony is firsthand and not secondhand
Require the contractor to produce the architect's written statement instead, which would serve as a more reliable form of evidence

rationale.a: Hearsay is admissible in administrative proceedings; relaxed standards apply.
rationale.c: Direct architect testimony is not required; hearsay testimony is admissible.
rationale.d: Written statement preference is not required; hearsay testimony suffices.
rationale.correct: Administrative hearings before the PRBoA apply relaxed evidentiary standards. Hearsay is admissible if relevant and offered for truth—establishing the architect's understanding of code applicability.
rationale.takeaway: Administrative hearings permit hearsay under relaxed evidentiary standards.

questions.text: An architect licensed in 2015 is accused of designing a building that does not comply with the 2023 Philippine Building Code. During the PRBoA investigation, the architect claims that when he was licensed and trained, different standards applied and he is not obligated to use 2023 standards. How should the PRBoA address this defense?

options.text: The claim is valid because architects can only be held to standards existing at the time of their original license, and changes are not retroactive
The claim is invalid because architects have an ongoing professional obligation to remain current with evolving standards
The PRBoA must prove the architect had actual notice of the 2023 standard changes, ensuring fair enforcement
Only architects licensed after 2023 must comply with the 2023 code, as it applies to new licenses only

rationale.a: Architects must stay current; original training standards do not excuse non-compliance.
rationale.c: Actual notice is not required; architects must independently maintain current knowledge.
rationale.d: All licensed architects must comply with current standards regardless of license date.
rationale.correct: Professional architects have continuous obligation to remain current with evolving codes and standards. The "I was trained differently" defense does not excuse non-compliance with current standards at the time of practice.
rationale.takeaway: Architects have continuous obligation to maintain current knowledge of evolving standards.

questions.code_citation: Code of Ethical Conduct; RA 9266 Section 22

questions.text: An architect successfully appeals a PRBoA suspension on the ground that the decision contained a clear legal error in interpreting Section 22 of RA 9266 (standard of care). The Court of Appeals agrees and reverses the suspension. Can the PRBoA reinvestigate the same facts and refile charges based on a different legal theory?

options.text: Yes, because the reversal only addresses the specific legal error, not the underlying conduct
Yes, if new evidence emerges during the reinvestigation
No, because double jeopardy principles in administrative law prevent relitigating the same facts
No, because the reversal constitutes an acquittal on the merits and precludes further action

rationale.b: New evidence is not required; existing facts may be pursued under different legal theory.
rationale.c: Strict double jeopardy limits apply in criminal contexts; administrative law is more flexible.
rationale.d: Reversal on legal error does not constitute acquittal on merits; facts may be relitigated.
rationale.correct: The reversal addresses legal error in law application, not factual findings. The underlying facts remain viable—the PRBoA may reinvestigate and pursue discipline under different legal theory if facts support it. Administrative law permits relitigation under different theories.
rationale.takeaway: Legal error reversal permits relitigation under different legal theory for same facts.

questions.text: Examine the appeal rights and limitations: A PRBoA decision finds the architect guilty of fraud (falsifying billing records) and revokes the license. The architect appeals to the Court of Appeals, which affirms. The architect then claims the court "made an error in not reconsidering the fraudulent intent finding." Is this ground sufficient for Supreme Court review?

options.text: Yes, because the Supreme Court reviews all administrative decisions on appeal, ensuring that justice is served in every case.
Yes, because fraud involves moral turpitude and constitutional due process, which are critical issues warranting higher court review.
No, because factual findings (including intent) are reviewed under substantial evidence standard and not reconsidered absent clear error
No, because the architect had a full opportunity to contest fraudulent intent at the PRBoA hearing, and procedural fairness was observed.

rationale.a: Supreme Court does not review all administrative decisions; discretionary review is limited.
rationale.b: Fraud and due process concerns do not automatically grant Supreme Court review; legal error must be demonstrated.
rationale.d: Opportunity at hearing does not change the appellate standard or discretionary review availability.
rationale.correct: Court of Appeals applies deferential substantial evidence standard on factual findings and does not reweigh evidence or reconsider credibility. Factual reassessment (including intent findings) does not meet discretionary review grounds.
rationale.takeaway: Factual findings reviewed under substantial evidence standard; reassessment not ground for review.

questions.text: An architect under investigation by the PRBoA fails to file an answer to the complaint within the required 15-day period. What is the consequence?

options.text: The complaint is automatically dismissed for lack of proper notice, unless the PRBoA decides to extend the deadline
The PRBoA must extend the deadline and provide another 15 days, allowing the architect additional time to respond
The architect waives the right to respond and facts may be presumed true; the case may proceed to recommended discipline
The architect is required to appear before the PRBoA to explain the delay, potentially facing further disciplinary action

rationale.a: Failure to answer does not dismiss the complaint; it forfeits the defense.
rationale.b: Extension is discretionary, not mandatory; failure to respond timely has consequences.
rationale.d: Appearance to explain delay is not required; the default consequence applies.
rationale.correct: Failure to file timely answer results in waiver of defense rights and adverse inference that allegations are true. This procedural default has serious consequences and can support discipline recommendation even without hearing.
rationale.takeaway: Failure to file timely answer waives defense rights and permits adverse inference.

questions.text: Compare two disciplinary scenarios: (1) Architect A failed to include required technical specifications in working drawings, causing a contractor claim; and (2) Architect B deliberately falsified structural calculations to meet an impossible budget. How would the PRBoA likely distinguish the severity of discipline?

options.text: Both would receive identical penalties because the violation category is the same, regardless of intent or potential impact on public safety.
Architect A's negligence might warrant probation or brief suspension, while Architect B's fraud would warrant suspension or revocation
Architect B's deliberate falsification would only warrant a fine because no physical harm occurred, unless it can be shown that the falsification led to a structural failure.
The PRBoA cannot consider intent—only whether the violation occurred, which means both cases are treated equally under the board's disciplinary guidelines.

rationale.a: Violation category does not determine identical penalties; intent and severity matter.
rationale.c: Fraud warrants serious discipline regardless of physical harm; financial/ethical harm suffices.
rationale.d: The PRBoA considers intent as a sentencing factor along with violation facts.
rationale.correct: The PRBoA considers intent and severity when determining discipline. Negligent omission (A) is less severe than fraudulent falsification (B), warranting proportionally lighter discipline.
rationale.takeaway: Fraud receives harsher discipline than negligence; intent affects sentencing severity.

questions.text: The PRBoA investigation report recommends dismissal of a complaint against an architect based on finding insufficient evidence of the alleged code violation. However, the PRBoA board members review the same evidence and conclude it supports the violation. What is the legal effect of the board's disagreement with the investigator?

options.text: The report is binding and the complaint must be dismissed
The board must follow the investigator's recommendation or explain why in writing
The board may reject the recommendation and proceed to hearing based on its independent review
The disagreement requires automatic appeal to the Court of Appeals

rationale.a: The report is not binding; the board has independent review authority.
rationale.b: The board need not follow the investigator's recommendation; only provide reasoning in decision.
rationale.d: Board disagreement with investigator is not automatic appeal ground.
rationale.correct: The investigator's report is advisory, not binding. The PRBoA board has independent authority to review evidence and reach its own conclusions—the board may disagree with recommendations.
rationale.takeaway: Investigator's report is advisory; PRBoA has independent review and decision authority.

questions.text: An architect receives notice that the PRBoA has suspended her license for 2 years based on a finding that she failed to provide adequate structural coordination. The architect believes this finding is clearly wrong based on the documentation submitted. Which remedy is most appropriate?

options.text: Request immediate reinstatement from the PRBoA before suspension takes effect, citing procedural errors in the initial hearing
File an appeal with the Court of Appeals within 30 days of decision promulgation
Demand a new PRBoA hearing on the factual issue, arguing that new evidence has come to light
Petition the Supreme Court for reversal of the suspension, emphasizing constitutional rights violations

rationale.a: Reinstatement must come through appeal or PRBoA reconsideration, not emergency request.
rationale.c: Court of Appeals review is the first appellate level; new PRBoA hearing is not the remedy.
rationale.d: Supreme Court is available only for exceptional cases; Court of Appeals is the proper first appeal.
rationale.correct: Appeal to Court of Appeals within 30 days is the proper remedy. The court reviews whether factual findings are supported by substantial evidence—the appropriate forum for challenging factual determinations.
rationale.takeaway: Court of Appeals appeal within 30 days is the proper remedy for PRBoA decisions.

questions.text: An architect suspended for 3 years due to a finding of gross negligence wishes to appeal the PRBoA decision. The architect's appeal brief argues the discipline is "excessive" and "unjust." However, the appeal brief provides no analysis of legal errors in the PRBoA's application of RA 9266 or the Code of Ethics. What is the likely outcome of the appeal?

options.text: The Court of Appeals will overturn the suspension because the architect questions the justice of the decision, despite lacking legal error analysis
The Court of Appeals will remand for a new PRBoA hearing, considering procedural fairness and potential oversight
The Court of Appeals will affirm because the appeal raises no legal error; excessive penalty arguments without legal error basis are unlikely to succeed
The Supreme Court will grant discretionary review because the matter involves professional discipline and may set a precedent

rationale.a: Justice disagreement without legal error does not overturn decisions.
rationale.b: Legal error in hearing procedures would warrant remand, but the brief raises only penalty disagreement.
rationale.d: Supreme Court discretionary review addresses exceptional cases, not ordinary penalty disputes.
rationale.correct: Appeals are limited to legal errors in law application and procedure. Disagreement with penalty without legal error does not succeed—the court presumes PRBoA decisions correct absent demonstrated legal error.
rationale.takeaway: Appeal success requires legal error; penalty disagreement alone does not prevail.
